lessons.title: Inspection decisions and final trimming
lessons.html:
After the meat inspector

Every sheep and goat carcass, with its head and organs, is inspected by the meat inspector. This is post-mortem inspection. The inspector may:

  • Pass the carcass: it is fit for people to eat.
  • Pass with trimming: some parts must be removed first.
  • Detain it: it goes to the detain rail for more examination. Do not touch it without permission.
  • Condemn it, in whole or in part: it is not fit to eat and goes to the condemned area.

You must always follow the inspector's decision.

Final trimming

The final trimmer makes the carcass clean and neat:

  • Remove any wool, hair, dirt or dung spots with a sterile knife.
  • Remove bruises and blood clots.
  • Remove the parts the meat inspector marked.
  • Trim the neck (sticking area) and any ragged pieces.
  • Do not trim more than needed; trimming removes valuable meat.

Put trimmings in the correct containers: edible trimmings separately from condemned material.

Final wash

Wash the carcass with clean, potable water, from top to bottom, to remove blood and bone dust. Washing must not be used to remove wool or dung; those are trimmed off. Do not soak the carcass; too much water spoils the appearance and can spread germs.

lessons.title: Weighing, classification and marking
lessons.html:
Weighing

Each carcass is weighed on the rail scale. The mass is recorded against the carcass number and the owner. Farmers are paid by mass and class, so mistakes cost money.

  • Check that the scale reads zero with an empty hook or as your plant procedure says.
  • Make sure the carcass hangs freely and does not touch anything while it is weighed.
  • Check that the number on the carcass matches the record.

Classification

In South Africa, red meat carcasses are classified by age and fatness under the national classification system. For small stock, a trained, registered classifier looks at the teeth to judge age (for example, lamb versus older animals) and at the fat cover. The carcass is then marked with a roller mark.

  • Only trained and authorised classifiers classify and mark.
  • Your job may be to present the carcass correctly and record the class.

Inspection stamp

Carcasses that the meat inspector has passed are stamped with the abattoir's approved inspection mark. Only authorised people use the stamp. A carcass without the mark must not leave the abattoir.

Records

Kill sheets record: date, owner, carcass number, mass, class and any condemnations. Fill in records clearly and honestly. The farmer, the buyer and the inspectors rely on them.

lessons.title: Chilling, storage and dispatch
lessons.html:
Chilling

Carcasses are warm after slaughter. Germs grow fast on warm meat, so carcasses must be moved into the chiller promptly. Your plant sets the target temperatures and times.

  • Hang carcasses with space between them so that cold air can move around each one.
  • Carcasses must not touch each other, the walls or the floor.
  • Do not overload the chiller. Put new warm carcasses where your plant procedure says, so they do not warm up the cold ones.
  • Keep chiller doors closed.
  • Check and record chiller temperatures as required. Report problems at once.

Storage

  • Keep passed carcasses away from detained or condemned material.
  • Keep offal in its own chilled area, in clean containers.
  • Only authorised people enter the chiller. Wear clean clothing and a hairnet.

Dispatch

  1. Check the order: which carcasses, how many, for which customer.
  2. Check that the truck is clean and cold before loading.
  3. Hang carcasses on the truck rails; never put them on the floor.
  4. Handle with clean hands and clean clothing.
  5. Complete the dispatch note and get it signed.

Safety in the chiller

  • Wear warm clothing and non-slip boots.
  • Know how to open the door from the inside.
  • Get help with heavy carcasses; use the rails.

Key points

  • Always follow the meat inspector's decision: pass, trim, detain or condemn.
  • Trim off wool and dung; wash only to remove blood and bone dust.
  • Weigh accurately and check carcass numbers against the records.
  • Only authorised people classify, mark and stamp carcasses.
  • Chill quickly with space around every carcass and record temperatures.
  • Load only into clean, cold trucks.

It is given back to the farmer

Age (judged from the teeth) and fatness

So cold air can move around each carcass
